passage:
Wasim, sit down. You answered that client at midnight again, didn't you? Let me tell you about me as a young man of twenty-five. I was the first engineer in the office to get a laptop, and I thought answering fast made me important. I'd reply to mails at eleven, twelve, sometimes one. Then I'd lie in bed with my mind still running spreadsheets. Your aunty would say, "Jomon, you're here, but you're not here."
One morning I fell asleep in a client meeting. My boss laughed it off, but I was mortified.
That week I told my team: after nine, only real emergencies, by call. I shut the laptop and walked with your aunty after dinner. The work didn't collapse. And I slept like a boy again.

qa.q: What did Jomon tell the team after that week?
qa.a: Jomon told them that after nine, only real emergencies, by call.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after falling asleep in the client meeting?
qa.a: Jomon felt mortified and embarrassed, even though the boss laughed it off.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jomon's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Setting a clear rule with the team and shutting the laptop after dinner gave Jomon's mind time to calm down before sleep.

qa.q: How did Jomon's late emails affect the aunty in the story?
qa.a: The aunty felt Jomon was present in body but distant in mind, saying 'you're here, but you're not here.'

passage:
The monsoon had knocked out power twice that week in Guwahati, and Tanvir's project was already behind. Worse, the client was in California, so messages arrived just as he was brushing his teeth. He'd reply, then lie awake rewriting his answers in his head, and drag himself up at seven feeling foggy.
On Thursday his manager Bhupen noticed him yawning through stand-up. "You were online at two," Bhupen said. "That's not a badge."
"They only reply at night."
"Then we set one overlap hour in the evening and they wait for the rest."
Tanvir set an away message, charged his phone in the living room and read a paper novel by torchlight when the power cut again. By Monday he woke before the alarm.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir charge his phone?
qa.a: He charged his phone in the living room.

qa.q: What was on Tanvir's mind as he lay awake?
qa.a: He was anxious about the work, rewriting his answers in his head instead of resting.

qa.q: Which choice helped Tanvir, and why?
qa.a: Agreeing one evening overlap hour and setting an away message gave him a clear boundary, so his mind could switch off before bed.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Tanvir being online at two?
qa.a: Bhupen sees it as a problem rather than dedication, and wants him rested.

grounding: It shows a professional whose late-night messages keep the mind buzzing, and how clear work boundaries and a screen-free wind-down help.

'Pema, it's eleven-thirty. Are you still working?'
'Just replying to the client. And the manager. And the group.'
Hansa put down her tea. 'You said that at nine.'
'I know. But if I don't reply, they'll think I'm slacking.'
'Then you lie awake till two, right? I hear you tossing.'
Pema rubbed her eyes. 'My brain keeps drafting emails when I close my eyes.'
'What time does your contract say you finish?'
'Six-thirty.'
'So what if you reply till eight, and then the laptop goes in the cupboard? You can say so in your signature.'
'That's scary.'
'So is waking up tired every day.'
Pema shut the laptop slowly. 'Okay. Starting tomorrow. And half an hour of no screens before bed.'

qa.a: Six-thirty.

subtype: Working screens late into the night [Actor]
passage: When I started at the design studio, my manager Damini sent messages at midnight, and I answered every one within minutes. I thought that was what being good at the job looked like. I'm Vandana, and for about six months I went to bed with my phone buzzing on the pillow. Even when it was quiet, my mind kept buzzing, rehearsing replies. I woke up every morning feeling I hadn't slept at all. One evening I asked Damini, nervously, whether she expected instant replies at night. She looked surprised. 'No! I just send them when I think of them.' After that I turned notifications off at nine and put the phone in the other room at ten-thirty. The first week felt wrong. Now I sleep through, and my work is actually better.

qa.q: When did Damini send messages?
qa.a: At midnight.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel in the mornings during those six months?
qa.a: Vandana felt unrested and drained, as if there had been no sleep at all.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Asking Damini about expectations, then turning notifications off at nine and moving the phone to another room at ten-thirty.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt learning Vandana replied at midnight?
qa.a: Damini was surprised and probably a little concerned, not having meant to pressure anyone.

grounding: Shows a professional replying to messages late at night whose mind keeps buzzing, and who sets work boundaries and a screen-free time before sleep.

Team lead's note, Monday
I've noticed Aadhya replying to client emails at 1 am, sometimes later. In meetings she looks pale, loses track of points and admitted she 'can't switch off' even when she stops working. She said she worries clients will think we're slow. I told her clearly: our working hours end at seven, and a morning reply is fine for almost everything. We agreed she'll set an out-of-hours auto-reply, silence work apps at eight, and keep the last half hour before bed screen-free. I'm also changing my own habit of sending late messages, since she may be copying me. We'll check in on Friday.
Devika

qa.a: Aadhya might keep feeling pressure to reply at night, since she may be copying the team lead.

Thursday, 12:15 a.m.
Answered Gurleen's "quick question" at 10:50. Then one more email to the Delhi client. Then tidied a slide nobody asked me to tidy. Now the lights are off and my brain is still running the spreadsheet, row by row. Woke up yesterday feeling like I'd slept in a bus seat. Snapped at the chaiwala for giving me change in coins. Not fair to him. At lunch today I asked Gurleen straight out whether late replies were expected. Gurleen looked surprised: "No! I just send things when I think of them. Answer in the morning." So all this was me. New rule from tonight: laptop shut at 9:30, work chat muted, then half an hour of washing up and music before bed.
Vinita
